name: Westside Barbell
who: Private, invite-only powerlifting gym founded by Louie Simmons, birthplace of the Conjugate Method.
why: Produced more elite raw and equipped powerlifting world records than any gym in history; the sport's acknowledged mecca.
takeaway: You cannot drop in — but you can run its conjugate method: rotate max-effort and dynamic days.

name: EliteFTS Compound
who: Dave Tate's training compound and equipment-company headquarters, the other pole of American powerlifting alongside Westside.
why: Decades of educational content, sponsored lifters, and the elitefts media machine make it a reference point for the whole strength-training industry.
takeaway: Treat it as a classroom — decades of Dave Tate's educational strength content live on this training floor.

name: Untamed Strength
who: Alan Thrall's strongman/powerlifting gym in Sacramento, built around raw barbell training and heavy YouTube documentation.
why: Thrall's instructional videos turned an ordinary local gym into one of the most-watched strength channels in the world.
takeaway: Watch the raw barbell fundamentals Alan Thrall built into one of the most-watched strength channels in the world.

name: Boss Barbell Club
who: Powerlifting-focused gym in Silicon Valley owned and coached day-to-day by 10x world-record raw powerlifter Dan Green.
why: One of the few US gyms run hands-on by an active elite competitor; the anchor of the Northern California powerlifting scene.
takeaway: Rare chance to train under an active 10x world-record powerlifter who coaches the floor himself.

name: Barbell Brigade
who: 5,500 sq ft powerlifting and strength-sports gym in downtown LA with 16 squat racks, 11 benches, and its own apparel/media brand.
why: Hosts USAPL and USPA meets on-site and built one of the largest powerlifting-apparel followings out of a single physical gym.
takeaway: Catch a USAPL or USPA meet on-site, then train on the same racks that host them.

name: Allegiate Gym
city: Los Angeles, California (Century City / Santa Monica)
who: High-end strength & conditioning studio group founded by former Army West Point strength coach Tim Caron, floors equipped with Eleiko, Sorinex, and Kabuki gear.
why: Brings Division-1-level programming and force-plate testing tech (GymAware, ForceDecks, NordBord) into a boutique-membership model.
takeaway: Expect Division-1-level programming and force-plate testing tech — GymAware, ForceDecks, NordBord — inside a boutique membership.

name: California Strength
who: Olympic weightlifting gym and coaching program, one of the longest-running dedicated weightlifting clubs in the US.
why: Coached multiple national-level weightlifters over nearly two decades and remains a reference program for USAW-style training.
takeaway: Learn USAW-style Olympic lifting from one of the longest-running dedicated weightlifting clubs in the country.

name: Hybrid Performance Method Gym
who: 24-hour private strength facility in Wynwood built for powerlifting, Olympic weightlifting, strongman and combat conditioning, home to Team HYBRID.
why: Founder Hayden Bowe's training app and podcast audience funnels a large online following toward one physical floor.
takeaway: Expect a mix of powerlifting, Olympic lifting, strongman and combat conditioning under Hayden Bowe's Team HYBRID banner.

name: Sorinex Strength Compound
who: Manufacturing headquarters and private training facility of Sorinex, the strength-equipment maker used by NFL, NBA and major college athletic departments.
why: World-unique showroom/training floor that visiting college strength coaches and pro athletes treat as a pilgrimage stop for equipment and technique.
takeaway: Go for the equipment as much as the training — visiting strength coaches treat this showroom as a pilgrimage stop.

name: American Iron Gym
who: Powerlifting and Olympic weightlifting gym owned by Bob and Tammy Lopes, running for over three decades.
why: One of Nevada's oldest dedicated barbell-sport gyms, a regional institution for USAPL and USAW lifters.
reach: presence confirmed, follower count not verified this session (2026-08)
takeaway: Train barbell sport at a three-decade Nevada institution built for serious USAPL and USAW lifters.

name: Thor's Power Gym
who: Strongman gym built by Hafthor Bjornsson ('The Mountain'), fitted with equipment custom-made by Rogue Fitness for his own training.
why: A genuine pilgrimage stop for strongman tourists in Iceland, doubling as a small museum of Bjornsson's world-record lifts and trophies.
takeaway: Study the custom Rogue equipment Bjornsson built for himself, and browse the trophy wall of his world records.

name: Strength Asylum
who: 13,500 sq ft bodybuilding/strongman gym in Stoke-on-Trent, training base of former World's Strongest Man Eddie Hall.
why: One of the best-known strongman gyms in the UK; Eddie Hall's decade-long membership put it on the map internationally.
takeaway: Check out the strongman setup Eddie Hall trained in for a decade — his membership put this gym on the map.

name: Metroflex Gym
who: Hardcore gym owned by Brian Dobson, best known as Ronnie Coleman's early training base and a long-running hub for elite raw squatters and deadlifters.
why: Straddles bodybuilding and powerlifting history; few gyms have produced this concentration of world-record lifts under one roof.
reach: follower count not verified this session (approx 2026)

name: Underground Strength Gym
who: Zach Even-Esh's strength gym for athletes, built on old-school barbell, sandbag and kettlebell training rather than machines.
why: Its coaching methodology and long-running content library shaped a generation of high-school and college strength coaches.
reach: follower count not verified this session (approx 2026)
takeaway: Skip the machines — train the old-school barbell, sandbag and kettlebell system that shaped a generation of strength coaches.

name: Doherty's Gym
who: Old-school, multi-generation strength and bodybuilding gym, one of Australia's longest-running hardcore gyms.
why: A rare surviving link to Australia's early powerlifting and strongman scene, still run as a no-frills barbell gym.
reach: follower count not verified this session (approx 2026)
takeaway: Open every day of the year — this has been the default base for Australia's competitive lifting scene for decades.
